The surface framework's client half, taught — what W4 added

Pedagogy·seedling·JUL 06, 2026

A plain-words primer on the surface features the switch added to @kolu/surface* — the active-connection manager, connectionScoped, createKeyedRoot, the accessor-shaped provider, entry-scoped registry cells, and honest teardown — with kolu's remaining policy layer as the worked example.

Contents

  • The volatility being tamed (why this belongs in the framework at all)
  • The six additions, ground up
  • Secondary: what’s left in kolu (the first consumer)
  • The through-line, if you read both notes

This is the companion to the hosting side, taught. That note taught the framework’s server half — how a surface crosses a machine, ending at buildHostRegistry (“hold a session per host, dispatch by name”). This note teaches what W4 added to the framework: the client half of the same story. The subject here is @kolu/surface*; kolu itself appears only at the end, as the first consumer.

The one-line map: the framework already owned “a server holds N live connections” (the registry). W4 made it own the mirror image — “a client holds N live connections, exactly one active, and the active one can swap at runtime” — plus everything that swap must not break.“Exactly one active” is today’s special case, not a ceiling (srid asked). The general volatility — a changing SET of live connections with a changing active SUBSET (the hybrid-canvas future) — is deliberately not a receptacle yet: its first real consumer is demand-gated. But the W4 shapes leave the door open by construction: the misroute guard is multiplicity-safe (each connection owns its own socket and clients — calls can’t cross), createKeyedRoot composes N-wise, and the two single-active composites encode it as policy, not physics — the manager’s retire-on-switch relaxes to retire-on-remove, and connectionScoped gains a set-shaped sibling (one scope per member). When hybrid canvas earns itself, multi-active is a relaxation of these primitives, not a rewrite. Six additions, each below with the problem that forced it.

The volatility being tamed (why this belongs in the framework at all)

A client that can live-switch connections faces one hard volatility: connection lifetime racing user intent. Subscriptions were opened against connection A; the user picks B; A’s socket is closing while B’s is warming; calls are in flight on both; and the UI must never show A’s data under B’s name. None of that is app-specific — any multi-connection client (kolu’s host switch today, a fleet view tomorrow) faces exactly it. That’s the framework test from the hosting note passing in the other direction: this is electricity, not app code.

The six additions, ground up

1 · createKeyedRoot<K, T> — the atom (surface/solid). Problem: “when this key changes identity, tear down everything the old key built and rebuild for the new one” — with the first value available synchronously (a render must never see undefined). It sounds trivial; it had been hand-rolled twice with two different bugs waiting (one copy tested, one not). Shape: createKeyedRoot(key, factory) — dispose-and-recreate a reactive root on key-identity change. The final review then found solid-js itself ships the guarantee — the implementation is now a thin alias over solid’s own mapArray (~20 lines of hand-rolled dispose bookkeeping deleted), it lives one layer down in @kolu/surface/solid (it’s pure solid-generic), and calling it without a reactive owner throws the documented contract instead of silently leaking. Everything else in this note stands on it. Kolu usage: never called directly — kolu reaches it through additions 2 and 4 (both are built on it), which is the point: one tested implementation of the guarantee, zero copies in app code.

2 · connectionScoped — subscriptions that survive a swap (surface/solid). Problem: a subscription opened against the active connection must tear down and re-open when the active connection changes — and a torn-down subscription must be silent. The bug that forced the invariant: the readout subscriptions were wrapped in a detached reactive root whose disposer was discarded, so a swap disposed the owner but never the subscription — it leaked live, caught the old socket’s dying error, and fired three red “server restarted” toasts on every switch.The honest debugging story, kept because it teaches: the first instinct was to filter the error at the subscribe site — a band-aid. The question “why isn’t the abort signal already catching this?” exposed the truth: the sub was never disposed at all. Two framework fixes fell out: the detached root’s disposer is now tied to the caller’s owner — a dance the final review then recognized as @solid-primitives/rootless’s createSubRoot and replaced with the library — and the abort signal now travels all the way into the stream source so a pending read cancels immediately (fixing an asymmetry — the reactive sibling already passed its signal). The invariant, named: a disposed subscription cannot report anything. Shape: connectionScoped(active, factory) — keyed on the connection’s identity, synchronously populated, owner-safe. When to reach for it: any .use()-style standing subscription in an app whose connection can swap. Kolu usage — bindingScoped is literally the manager’s connectionScoped re-exported, and every standing readout rides it:

// packages/client/src/binding/bindings.ts — the framework primitive IS kolu's helper:
export const bindingScoped = manager.connectionScoped;

// packages/client/src/kaval/KavalUpdateBadge.tsx — a real consumer: this kaval-status
// sub re-opens against the new host's padi on every switch, old one torn down + silent:
const kavalStatus = useBindingScopedSub((b) =>
  b.clients.padi.cells.daemonStatus.use(...));

And the second name in that snippet, glossed: useBindingScopedSub is kolu’s shared-singleton form of bindingScoped — createSharedRoot(() => bindingScoped(pick)), composed from the framework primitive plus kolu’s pre-existing createSharedRoot. The problem it solves: bindingScoped runs under some reactive owner, and for an app-wide standing readout (daemon status, memory, inventory) the owner must be neither a component (unmounting would kill the sub out from under every other consumer) nor duplicated (N components opening N identical subscriptions). The shared root gives the sub one app-lifetime owner shared by every consumer — and you read it as plain useX(): the helper derefs the shared root internally, so the unavoidable double-read lives in exactly one commented place inside it and no consumer ever writes the signal-of-signal useX()() shape (srid caught that hack; the final review killed every such call site). Framework mechanism, kolu ownership policy — which is why it lives in binding/, not in surface-app.

3 · createActiveConnectionManager<K, C> — the client-side twin of the registry (surface-app/solid). Problem: someone must own the keyed cache of live connections, the one-active rule, and the switch itself — and the switch has two failure modes that look exotic until they bite. The yank: warming a new connection can take seconds (an ssh provision); a naive await warm(); setActive(k) means an abandoned pick commits late and yanks the user away from their newer choice. The manager owns a pick epoch — bumped as the first statement (before even the same-key early return, so re-picking the current key cancels an in-flight pick), re-checked after every await: last intent wins, always. The misroute: a call in flight on the old connection must not resolve against it while the UI shows the new one — switching retires the old connection (socket closed, send stubbed to throw a typed, honest “retired by this client” error — never a fake “server restarted”). Shape: the manager takes policy callbacks — how to build a connection, how to warm it, how to word a failure — and owns all the mechanism, including enacting the server-rejection fallback itself (the callback only notifies; the review found a policy hook that had to reach back into mechanism forced a forward-reference dance at the call site, so the enaction moved inside). It also runs each connection’s factory under its own manager-owned reactive root and tracks retirement internally — a consumer’s connection type is just { dispose() }. Kolu usage — the entire host switch is this one construction plus policy (packages/client/src/binding/bindings.ts):

manager = createActiveConnectionManager<string, Binding>({
  initialKey: LOCAL_HOST,
  makeConnection: makeBinding,          // kolu's connectSurfaces bundle for ?host=<h>
  socketOf: (b) => b.ws,                // what to retire on switch
  isFallbackKey: (h) => h === LOCAL_HOST,
  fallbackKey: LOCAL_HOST,              // where a rejected host falls back to
  serverRejectedCloseCode: 1008,        // "host gone" → the MANAGER falls back itself
  warm: async (h, active) => {          // deliberate add-then-connect, via the
    await active.link.hosts.add({ host: h });  // CURRENT binding's link
  },
  onWarmError: /* toast — quiet if superseded by a newer pick */
  onServerRejected: /* toast ONLY — notification; the fallback is enacted above */
});
// switching a tab = manager.switchTo("zest") — epoch, retirement, re-key all inherited.

It is buildHostRegistry’s mirror image; the framework now holds both halves of “a changing set of live connections.”

4 · The provider goes accessor-shaped (surface-app). Problem: SurfaceAppProvider took its control-plane client as a static value — a page-lifetime assumption baked into the framework’s own front door. Shape: controlPlane: Accessor<ControlPlane<T>>; the provider re-derives its build-info subscription per control-plane identity (on createKeyedRoot, same guarantee, one tested home). Static callers just write () => client; swapping callers hand it the active connection’s accessor. Kolu usage (packages/client/src/index.tsx) — one JSX prop is the whole integration:

<SurfaceAppProvider controlPlane={() => activeBinding().clients.surfaceApp} …>
// a host switch re-derives build identity for the new host — no reload, no stale banner.

5 · Honest teardown as a typed fact (surface-app). Problem: a retired socket used to throw an error whose message claimed “server restarted — reload required” — a lie for an intentional switch, and downstream code toasted it. Two different states shared one representation. Shape: retirement now throws a distinct typed error (“socket retired by this client”); genuine stale-restart keeps its own. Distinct states, distinct types — the same rule as the identity sum in the hosting note. Kolu usage: nothing to call — kolu only tells the manager what to retire (socketOf: (b) => b.ws above) and inherits the honesty: a late call on a switched-away binding rejects with the retired-transport fact, the reload overlay fires only on a genuine server restart, and the old three-red-toasts lie is unspellable.

6 · Entry-scoped cells on buildHostRegistry (surface-nix-host). Problem: a registry entry often wants to serve its own diagnostic cells (identity, inventory) derived from its own session — and a hand-rolled side-map of disposers next to the registry disposed them on explicit removal but not on add-rollback or destroy-all: two latent leaks. Shape: HostEntry gains optional cells?: { dispose() }, and the registry disposes entry cells beside session.destroy() at every teardown site. Kolu usage (packages/server/src/hostPool.ts) — each pool entry serves its host’s own diagnostics and hands their lifecycle to the registry:

buildEntry: (host) => {
  const perHostKolu = buildPerHostKoluCells(host, session); // identity·convergence·inventory,
  return {                                                  // read from THIS host's session
    session,
    handler,
    cells: { dispose: perHostKolu.dispose }, // registry disposes at EVERY teardown site —
  };                                          // remove, add-rollback, destroyAll alike
},

The leak class is structurally gone — the lifecycle lives with the thing that owns the other teardowns.

Secondary: what’s left in kolu (the first consumer)

After the six additions, kolu’s own code shrinks to policy:

  • client/src/binding/ — which host (the activeHost signal + sessionStorage, per-tab by design), the Labs picker, recents, the toasts, the padi-flavored warm step (hosts.add through the current link), and useBindingScopedSub (the shared-singleton composition of the framework’s connectionScoped with kolu’s createSharedRoot — ownership policy, so it stays app-side). All the mechanism it used to hand-roll — cache, epoch, retirement, re-keying — is framework calls now (~150 lines deleted).
  • server/src/hostPool.ts — buildHostRegistry holding one DaemonSession<PadiSurfaceClient> per machine (local arm or ssh arm per host), each entry contributing its per-host cells via addition 6; no controls, so pool.reconnect doesn’t even typecheck.
  • The dialogs read identity()/convergence() off the active binding — per-host by construction.

That division is the point: the next multi-connection app (a fleet view is literally “N live mirrored clients whose set changes”) writes only the equivalent policy layer and inherits every bug-fix above for free.

The through-line, if you read both notes

The hosting note ended on: when your thing won’t fit a framework slot, check whether the behavior or only the annotation refuses — widen the slot if it’s the annotation. This note is the complementary rule: when an app grows machinery that tames a hard volatility, name the receptacle it wants and graduate it — the review’s job is to make the candidate visible even at a population of one. The server half grew buildHostRegistry (drishti proved it); the client half grew createActiveConnectionManager (kolu proved it); the framework now owns both halves, and both apps write policy.
